'''Joshua R Sanes''' (born 1949) is an American [[neurobiologist]] who is known for his contributions to the understanding of [[synapse]] development. Throughout his career, Sanes has been the recipient of various awards and honors, including membership in the [[U.S. National Academy of Sciences]]. His research involves an interdisciplinary approach which focuses mainly on the formation of synapses at the neuromuscular junction by combining the sciences of [[psychology]], [[chemistry]], [[biology]], and [[engineering]] to study these circuits and employing molecular and genetic imaging to understand their function. Sanes currently lives in [[Boston, Massachusetts]] with his wife, Susan, and their two children.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gruber.yale.edu/neuroscience/joshua-sanes|title=Joshua Sanes {{!}} Gruber Foundation|website=gruber.yale.edu|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2020-08-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803144114/https://gruber.yale.edu/neuroscience/joshua-sanes|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Sanes was born in [[Buffalo, New York]] in 1949. Sanes' father owned an automobile parts store, and his mother attended school to become a speech pathologist. His father and mother both loved to read and so they kept plenty of books around the house. This is what sparked Sanes interest in the brain at a young age, since popular books during the 1950s included those on psychology. During high school, this interest led him to work in a laboratory at the Buffalo Children's Hospital under the microbiologist [[Robert Guthrie (microbiologist)|Robert Guthrie]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Davis|first=T. H.|date=2004-12-27|title=Biography of Joshua R. Sanes|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=102|issue=1|pages=5–7|doi=10.1073/pnas.0408739102|pmid=15623553|pmc=544077|issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free}}</ref> They studied mental illnesses as it relates to bacteria. In addition to his laboratory work, as a student at Williamsville South Highschool, Sanes was editor of the school's newspaper, played cello in the orchestra, and was president of the Model U.N.

==Academic career and work ==
Sanes graduated from [[Yale]] in 1970 with degrees in Biochemistry and Psychology. He then went on to [[Harvard]] to earn his doctorate in [[Neurobiology]] in 1976. After he finished his doctorate, he left Harvard to pursue his interest in [[health policy]] in Washington, D.C., in the [[Office of Technology Assessment]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Marx|first=Vivien|date=2013-06-01|title=Joshua Sanes|journal=Nature Methods|language=en|volume=10|issue=6|pages=449|doi=10.1038/nmeth.2487|pmid=23866327|s2cid=34579392|issn=1548-7105|doi-access=free}}</ref>

After a year working for the U.S. Congress, Sanes wanted to continue his career studying neurobiology. He completed his postdoctoral work at the [[University of California at San Francisco]], and then spent over 20 years, from 1980 until 2004, working as a member of the faculty of [[Washington University School of Medicine]] in the department of [[physiology]]. In 2004, he moved to Harvard, and became the Director of the Center for Brain Science.<ref name=":0" /> He is currently a professor of Molecular and [[Cellular Biology]] at Harvard University.

==Research ==
[[File:Brainbow (Lichtman 2008).jpg|thumb|Brainbow]]
Professor Sanes' early research focused on the NMJ ([[neuromuscular junction]]); he was in particular interested in a protein that emanated from the motor neuron, [[agrin]]. With the aid of agrin-[[knockout mice]], he and his co-workers showed a particular form of agrin was required for formation of the NMJ.  
Professor Sanes' later research has focused on synapses that connect nerve cells and the function and formation of them. In particular, his work has been critical in understanding brain disorders. An important discovery he made in the field of neuroscience earlier in his career were the signals discovered in the [[extracellular matrix]] that were found to be crucial in organizing the synapse. That led to his most notable development, the creation of the [[brainbow]] mouse.<ref name=":1" /> This allowed his laboratory to fluorescently trace synapses with markers to yield high-quality, vivid images of brain activity. These brainbow line images have been examined around the world to determine specific neuronal pathways within the mosaic of neuron tangles in the brain. Additionally, over his career, Sanes has been a part of hundreds of published papers involving the study of synapses from molecular and [[embryological]] perspectives.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=sanes+jr|title=sanes jr - PubMed - NCBI|last=pubmeddev|website=www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov|language=en|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2022-10-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221023011111/https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=sanes+jr|url-status=live}}</ref> Most recently, Sanes lab is studying the function of neuronal circuits specifically in the [[retina]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/joshua-r-sanes-pv7fzn/|title=Joshua Sanes|website=www.nasonline.org|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2019-03-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190324141439/http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/20002153.html|url-status=live}}</ref> This plays an important role in [[visual processing]].

==Awards and honors==
Sanes has received many awards and honors throughout his career studying synapses and their function and formation. He is also known for his work as a mentor and teacher in the scientific community.

* Member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences
* Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* Received the Alden Spencer Award of [[Columbia University]] in 2000
* Recipient of the 2017 [[Gruber Neuroscience Prize]]
* 2019 Cowan Award for contributions in developmental neuroscience<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/10969861/homepage/cowan___palay_awards.htm|title=Journal of Comparative Neurology|website=Wiley Online Library|doi=10.1002/(ISSN)1096-9861|language=en|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2021-05-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210529055558/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/10969861/homepage/cowan___palay_awards.htm|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Awarded the [[Edward M. Scolnick Prize in Neuroscience]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://mcgovern.mit.edu/2020/02/05/joshua-sanes/|title=Joshua Sanes awarded the 2020 Scolnick Prize|date=2020-02-06|website=MIT McGovern Institute|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2020-03-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321095617/https://mcgovern.mit.edu/2020/02/05/joshua-sanes/|url-status=live}}</ref>
* Awarded Honorary Doctorate Degree by Hebrew University in Jerusalem<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/newsplus/joshua-r-sanes-recognized-by-hebrew-university/|title=Joshua R. Sanes recognized by Hebrew University|date=June 15, 2022|access-date=January 21, 2023|archive-date=January 22, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230122031822/https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/newsplus/joshua-r-sanes-recognized-by-hebrew-university/|url-status=live}}</ref>
* 2025 Foreign Member of the [[Royal Society]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-05-20 |title=Exceptional scientists elected as Fellows of the Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2025/05/new-fellows/ |access-date=2025-05-22 |website=Royal Society |language=en}}</ref>

In addition to various awards, Sanes also served on several advisory boards and committees, which included ones for the [[Max-Planck Institute]], the [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]], the [[Wellcome Trust]], and the [[National Institutes of Health]]. He served on the National Advisory Council of the National Institute of Neurological Diseases and Stroke, the Council of the Society for Neuroscience, the [[Muscular Dystrophy Association]], the Klingenstein Neuroscience Fund, the Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Association, the [[Stowers Institute]], and the Searle Scholars Fund.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mcgill.ca/crn/research/board|title=Scientific Advisory Board|website=Research in Neuroscience|language=en|access-date=2020-04-13|archive-date=2021-06-17|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210617024515/https://www.mcgill.ca/crn/research/board|url-status=live}}</ref>
